segments.speaker: assistant
segments.text: Red blood cells lack a cell wall and only have a flexible plasma membrane. In pure water (which has the highest water potential, 0 kPa), water enters the cell by osmosis, causing it to swell and eventually burst – a process called haemolysis. Plant cells, by contrast, possess a rigid cellulose cell wall. When water enters by osmosis, the membrane presses against this wall and the cell becomes turgid (turgor pressure) instead of bursting. In a hypertonic solution, plant cells lose water and the membrane pulls away from the wall, which is plasmolysis. Water always moves from higher to lower water potential; adding solute lowers water potential (makes it more negative).
